lines: I.  Introduction

A population of K·m items carries unknown values θᵢ and is partitioned into K groups. Each group g carries an unknown common offset b_g. Under a unit sampling budget the experimenter must return a threshold set — which items lie above a fixed level. The values themselves are not the goal; the answer is.

Two kinds of measurement are available, and the distinction between them is the entire subject of this work. An ORDINARY query on item i returns θᵢ + b_g(i) with noise of variance v at unit price; crucially it sees the item's value and its group's offset only in combination, never apart. A CALIBRATION query on group g returns the offset b_g directly, with variance ν, at price κ measured in units of an ordinary query.

Throughout, a = x/v is the ordinary precision purchased on an item, b = z/ν the control precision purchased on its group, Δ the separation between the two worlds to be distinguished, and s_m = √m, s_κ = √κ. A design is any non-negative allocation of the unit budget across query types and groups.

The dilemma is concrete. Calibration queries consume budget that could have bought ordinary samples. If they merely improve efficiency, a careful allocator can trade them off and the question is one of tuning. If instead there exist configurations on which no quantity of ordinary sampling can ever answer the question, then the trade-off framing is wrong: the calibration query is a precondition, not a refinement, and an allocator that economises on it fails outright rather than gracefully.

This work answers two questions and no others. WHEN does the calibration query stop being an efficiency gain and become mandatory? And WHAT does it cost — the exact optimal value under a unit budget, not an order of magnitude and not a rate up to unspecified constants.
II.  Contributions

C1.  A NECESSITY DICHOTOMY, WITH AN EXACT WITNESS. We exhibit two worlds, in exact rationals, that every ordinary query cannot tell apart while their answers differ. On such a configuration the attainable value is exactly zero. The calibration query is therefore a precondition for the problem to be solvable at all, not an efficiency option, and no quantity of ordinary sampling changes that.

C2.  THE EXACT PRICE OF ONE UNIT OF INFORMATION IN A GROUP. We prove that a group required to deliver profiled information h costs at least h(√m + √κ)², and we exhibit the split attaining it. The two query prices combine through their SQUARE ROOTS — the signature of a two-resource harmonic trade-off — and this constant is exact rather than an order of magnitude.

C3.  THE PRICE LAW, MATCHED ON BOTH SIDES AND ATTAINED. We prove Γ* = Δ²/(2K(√m+√κ)²) as an upper bound over EVERY unit-budget design, not over a parametric family, together with a design meeting it. The result is an identity in the structural parameters (K, m, κ), and it yields the operational crossover κ = m at which the two query types consume equal shares of each group's budget.

C4.  A CERTIFIED INSTANCE WHERE OMITTING THE QUERY IS STRICTLY WORSE. On one explicit instance we cap every anchor-free design at 1/8 — a bound that is itself attained, hence tight — and exhibit an anchored design reaching 261/1520, a gap of 37.4%. Both sides are exact rationals and the cap is stated for an abstract design type, so no optimality of the anchored design is assumed.

C5.  EVERY CLAIM MACHINE-CHECKED. Four Lean 4 modules, 29 audited declarations, no sorry, axioms confined to {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}. Numerical sweeps are reported separately from theorems and never substitute for one.
III.  Methodology
The argument is a chain of eight steps. Each states what is proved, how it was closed, and how it depends on the step before.
STEP 1 — THE DICHOTOMY  (contribution C1).   hidden_shift_means,  hidden_shift_answers_differ
Four items, two per group, are exhibited together with a second world reached by shifting one group and paying the shift back through its offset:

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Both conjuncts are finite rational identities discharged by case analysis over the four items. No analysis and no limiting argument enters: the first is checked item by item, the second is a disagreement between two explicitly computed finite sets.

Item 0 lies above threshold in the first world and below it in the second, while item 3 lies above in both — yet every ordinary query has an identical mean in the two worlds. The attainable value is exactly zero, not merely small.
STEP 2 — PROFILING THE GROUP OFFSET.   profiled_information,  profiled_information_form
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 1. Step 1 shows the offset must be measured. Step 2 asks what a measurement of it is worth, by eliminating the offset from the energy:

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Completing the square in the shift t, with both halves proved separately: the inequality for every t, and the value attained at t = aΔ/(a+b). The harmonic form on the right is the shape that propagates through the rest of the chain, and it is what makes Step 3 a statement about COST rather than about information.
STEP 3 — THE COST OF ONE GROUP, LOWER BOUND  (contribution C2).   group_cost_lower

WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 2. Step 2 fixes how much information a group delivers at given precisions. Step 3 inverts the question: a group required to deliver h obeys h(x+z) ≤ xz, and we ask what that costs at prices m and κ.

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Cauchy–Schwarz applied to (s_m x − s_κ z)², then division by the positive quantity x + z. No optimiser is run and no multiplier theorem is invoked; the inequality is elementary and holds for every feasible pair.
STEP 4 — THE COST OF ONE GROUP, ATTAINED  (contribution C2).   group_cost_attained
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 3. A lower bound alone leaves the constant unidentified. Step 4 exhibits the allocation meeting it, so the constant is exact and not merely valid.

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Substitution and rational algebra: the stated split makes the information constraint an equality and the budget expression collapses to h(√m + √κ)². Neither query type can be dropped without losing the group entirely.

Fig. 1.  The dichotomy of Step 1. Solid bars are item values θ, hatched bars the group offset b, and the black dashes mark what an ordinary query observes — identical in both worlds. The answers, read at threshold ½, are not.
III.  Methodology, continued
STEP 5 — THE K-GROUP UPPER BOUND  (contribution C3).   calibration_rate_upper
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 4. Step 4 prices one group; Step 5 sums that price across K groups and confronts it with the unit budget, converting a per-group cost into a cap on the whole design.
HOW IT IS CLOSED. The per-group bound is applied inside a finite sum, then the budget constraint is used once. The statement quantifies over EVERY unit-budget design, so no design escapes it.
STEP 6 — THE BOUND IS ATTAINED  (contribution C3).   calibration_rate_attained
Steps 5 and 6 are the two halves of an identity: a cap over all designs, and a design meeting it.

Free calibration recovers the cost of the ordinary queries alone; expensive calibration dominates the budget; at the crossover κ = m the two square roots are equal and each query type consumes exactly half of each group's budget.
STEP 7 — THE ANCHOR IS MANDATORY  (contribution C4).   anchorFree_le,  anchorFree_attained,  anchor_mandatory

WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 6. Step 6 prices a design that already includes the calibration query; Step 7 asks whether omitting it can ever be competitive, on one instance where both sides are computable exactly.

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The cap on anchor-free designs is a dual certificate valid for every such design and is itself attained, hence tight; the anchored value comes from an explicit design spending 9/20 + 9/20 + (1/10)·1 = 1. Both sides are exact rationals.
STEP 8 — GAIN FACTORISATION.   hadamard_square_factor,  min_attained_on_active
Step 5 assembles a K-group sum from per-group statements; Step 8 supplies the structural facts making that assembly legitimate without a separate convexity argument.
IV.  Results

THE LAW IS EXACT AND INDEPENDENT NUMERICS AGREE TO MACHINE PRECISION. Bisection and Nelder–Mead were run over the same feasible set in 32 parameter cells. The largest relative gap against the closed form is 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁶, and Nelder–Mead never exceeds the closed form in any cell — the direction that would falsify an upper bound.
REMOVING THE CONTROL QUERY GIVES EXACTLY ZERO. Over the same 32 cells, the no-control and one-control-missing baselines return exactly 0, by the Step 1 witness verified before any solver is called.
BAD ALLOCATION COSTS A BOUNDED FRACTION. A uniform design retaining all controls reaches 73.5–100% of the optimum, median 91.7%.

Fig. 2.  Control baselines over 32 parameter cells. Removing the control query yields exactly zero by the Step 1 witness rather than by numerical failure; a uniform design retaining all controls reaches 73.5–100% of the optimum.
V.  Discussion

The two results above are asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the practical message. An experimenter who allocates badly loses a bounded fraction of the attainable information; an experimenter who omits the query TYPE loses everything, and no amount of sampling recovers it. Efficiency and feasibility are therefore not points on one scale, and a procedure treating the calibration query as one more option to trade off cannot detect the failure.

The crossover κ = m gives a concrete rule. Below it, ordinary sampling dominates the budget and calibration is cheap insurance; above it, the calibration query is the binding cost and the group size m is what must be reconsidered.

SCOPE — WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The law assumes a common variance v, a common control variance ν, a common price κ and equal gaps; heterogeneous cases are not covered. Step 7 certifies ONE instance: it proves anchor-free designs CAN be strictly beaten, not that they always are. Step 1 exhibits two indistinguishable worlds without characterising all such configurations. Everything here is an information and budget statement — no estimator, no confidence set and no finite-sample guarantee is claimed.
VI.  Conclusions

A calibration query is not an efficiency improvement a careful allocator could do without. On the configurations exhibited here the attainable value is exactly zero until a query of the new type is bought; once bought, its price is exact, matched by a lower bound, an upper bound over all unit-budget designs, and an attaining design.

Formal corpus behind this poster

The 9 displayed equations are the load-bearing chain, not the corpus. The MASTER strand contains 11 Lean source files with 88 theorem and lemma statements, of which 7 modules carry an acceptance receipt covering 57 declarations whose axiom set was printed and checked. Across the whole programme: 427 files, 3,115 statements, 108 accepted modules, 860 audited declarations.

Every audited declaration was checked to depend only on {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}. No module cited by any gate in this work contains a sorry: the seven that exist in the wider repository sit in audit scaffolding and in files named as conjectures, and the overlap with the cited set is empty.

What the poster shows is the shortest path from the problem statement to the claim. The remaining statements are the machinery that path stands on — arithmetic lemmas, measurability side conditions, finite-sum exchanges and the counterexamples that ruled out earlier formulations.
